- Hello, everyone, welcome
back to Altium Academy,
I'm your host, Zach Peterson.
Today, we're gonna be looking
at a practical example of via delay,
particularly in a parallel bus like DDR.

Now, this is a great
question that came to me

from my LinkedIn from
one of our superfans,

and so, of course, I'm
very happy to go over it
with you all today.

So let's go ahead and
jump in and get started.
(upbeat music continues)
Now, the topic of this video is via delay
or propagation delay through vias,
and whether or not you need to include it

in length tuning calculations
in a parallel bus.

So let's take a look
at that viewer question
about this topic.
Superfan Zakaraya Oudaimah writes,
"Hello, Zach, I have a question

that was coming from your
YouTube channel about via delay.

I have a DDR3 DQ bus with
eight bits from an example,
I saw something in PCB routing
for high speed design that belongs
to DATA_BL0 DQS group one.
Some tracks are routed in layer 1
and others are routed in layer 2.

Is there any problem
with the via delay here

or should we always route
the lines in the same layer?
Or if we're routing in different layers,
should we calculate the via delay

of each via routed from
one layer to another?"

And then here he shows
some example routing.
Here we have our layer 1 routing,
and then you can see here

we have some net selected
on the next layer,

and then some additional net
selected on an inner layer.
You can see that this routing
for this DDR bus spans multiple layers.

Now, there are many
different parallel buses,

and because DDR is, of
course, a parallel bus,
it requires length tuning
across all of the traces in the bus.

And when you have to
provide length tuning,

what you're actually doing is
you're adjusting the timing.

So you're really doing delay
tuning, not length tuning,
and that means you need to include
all of those sources of delay

in the calculation of
the length that you need

in order to properly compensate
for SKU across the bus.
But do you really have to include
every single source of delay?
Well, of course, it depends.
It depends on how big those delays are
and how big of a margin you have

across the entire bus
for timing mismatches

on all of the different
signals in that bus.
So in order to illustrate

whether or not we need
to account for something
like via delay in these buses,
let's take a look at the propagation delay
on different strip line layers
that we might use for routing DDR,

and then compare that to, for
example, the propagation delay
that we might see on micros strip layers
or on the surface layers.

We can then take a look
at a simulation in Simbeor

to see what the typical
via delay value is,
and that's gonna allow us to judge
whether or not we really need to include

that delay value in our
length tuning calculations.

So let's consider a typical
stackup that we might use

for a high speed board
that has a lot of signals
including something like DDR.

So let's say, for example,
we have a 10-layer stackup,
and we have, for example,

L1 where we're gonna
have our micros strips,

we then have a ground
plane, which is typical,
we then have L3,

which is gonna be our
first strip line layer,

and then we're gonna
have some other layers.
And what I wanna do here is compare
the propagation delay values

on all of these different
layers to something like,
for example, layer 8.
And then here we have our ground plane,
and then we also have layer 10.

So first things first, do
we have to route everything
on just the same layer

or do we have to route
everything on different layers,

but then account for the different
propagation delay values?
First of all, if you just load up
the default 10 layer stackup

inside of the layer
stack manager in Altium,
that's gonna give you a sense
for the different propagation delay values

that you might expect in
these types of stackups.

So for example, let's
take a look at layer 1.

Layer 1 propagation delay in
that default 10 layer stackup

inside Altium has a value of
about 155 picoseconds per inch.

Now, let's compare that
to, for example, layer 3,
and then layer 8, and then layer 10.

Well, in the default stackup
in Altium designer, again,
this is going to be a symmetrical stackup,

so the layer thicknesses on
the top side are gonna be equal

to the layer thicknesses
on the bottom side.

So this one is also going to
be 155 picoseconds per inch.
Now, what about layer 3 and layer 8?
Well, layer 3 is going to have a value
of about 175 picoseconds per inch,
and then layer 8, again,

we have the symmetry
here that we can exploit,
so we know layer 8 also has

175 picoseconds per
inch propagation delay.

Now, again, this is the default
stackup in Altium Designer,
and if you use a different layer count,
you use different layer thicknesses,
you use different materials,
you're gonna get different values here.

But the point here is
just to be able to compare
the differences in micros strip layers
versus the strip line layers.
And these are the typical values
that you get in their default stackup.

They use core layers with,
I believe, DK equal 4.3,

and then we have pre-reg layers
with DK equal to about 4.1.

Now, if we're routing a
DDR bus on two layers,

let's say layer 1 and
layer 3, we already have

a 20-picoseconds per inch
propagation delay difference
in the routing on those two layers.

However, if we route
everything as strip lines
on two different layers,

which is actually a much
more typical situation,

then you'll see that we basically
get about the same values

for the propagation delays
on these two layers,

assuming that we have the
same material composition
in each of these regions.

Now, by default, your
routing tool is already going
to take account of these two values

if you're routing on layer
1 and layer 3, for example.

So it already knows the
propagation delay difference
when you set up an impedance profile
and it's gonna be able to account for
this 20 picoseconds per inch difference

in the propagation delay when
you're routing the traces.

Now, this 20 picoseconds per
inch value is significant

because the SKU tolerance
that you can accept
across the entire bus for DDR3 or DDR4
is gonna be somewhere in the neighborhood
of like 50 picoseconds,
so it's actually a pretty small value.
Now, with a 20-picoseconds difference,

if you routed two inches of
trace on both of these layers,

you can already see that
you've almost entirely eaten up

that 50 picosecond margin
that you can accept
for SKU across these two layers.

This is why we might
prefer to route everything

as strip lines or
everything as micros strips
and then use some vias to reach the chip
on one of the two surface layers.
Now, this just accounts for the traces,
but what about the vias?
If we're routing on different layers,
we're gonna have to route through vias

in order to reach the chip,
let's say on the top layer.
And if we have the chip on the top layer,

but we're routing through
the internal layers,
then we're gonna have some differences

in the propagation
distance for these vias.

And because, of course,
the distances are different
from layer 1 to the top layer
versus layer 8 to the top layer,
or from the bottom to the top layer,

we're then gonna have
different via delay values

that we might expect for
routing from one of these layers

up to the top side where
we might have our chip.
So how do we calculate via delay?
And then once we calculate it,

how do we include it in
the time delay calculation

that the routing tool uses
inside of our CAD tool?
Well, in another video,

I actually presented a simple
model from Howard Johnson

in his Black Magic
textbook, which runs over
how to calculate this.

The problem is that even the
author Howard Johnson admits
that the model is objectively wrong.

You can use that model
to calculate via delay

for frequencies where the via
delay doesn't really matter
and it's probably going to be accurate.

But in this case where you
have a high speed parallel bus

that has a pretty tight
tolerance on the SKU allowance,
you're gonna have to figure out
this via delay from a simulation.
Now, there are some calculators that claim
to give you the correct via delay,

but the reality is, you'll
have to use a 3D simulator

or a simulation tool that has
specialized models for vias
and use that to get the via delay.
The other thing you can do is you can take
S parameter measurements.
And from S parameter measurements

or simulations that give
you the S parameter,
you can calculate the via delay
from the insertion loss spectrum from via.
Now, what I want to do is take a look
at an example in Simbeor.
And what we'll do is we'll get some ideas
for how big those via delays are

when we're routing from
different internal layers
up to a surface layer.
So here we are inside of Simbeor,

and I have a simple via
analyzer project pulled up.

And this via project is set
up for a six-layer stackup.

And so what I'm gonna do here
is just show you the values
that we get to give you kind of an idea

of an order of magnitude of
the via delays you can expect

when you're routing
between different layers.
So here in the via that I have pulled up,
we're routing between layer 1 and 2,

and then I have an identical
via pulled up here,
but we're routing between 1 and 4.
Now, one of the nice things about Simbeor

is it actually just gives
you the via delay directly.
You don't have to manually calculate it
from an insertion loss plot.
Now, of course, you can calculate it
from the insertion loss plot if you want,
but you're not required to.

But let's take a look at
this first example via

where we're routing between
layer 3 and layer 1.

So you can see here, if
I just hold my mouse,
it gives you the delay at 48 gigahertz.

It tells you that a delay
is three picoseconds.
This is one of the things that's important
about insertion loss plots is, of course,

insertion loss will tell
you that the via delay

or the propagation delay
in general is not going
to be the same at all frequencies,

and that's what this calculator
is gonna tell us as well.

But again, it does give
us an order of magnitude
of the value that we can expect.

So here you can see that
it's three picoseconds delay

for one of these vias
across the layers spanning
from layer 1 to layer 3.

Now, what if we go from
layer 1 to layer 4?
Well, that's gonna be this via,
and you can see here one of my ports moved
down here to layer 4.
If I hold my mouse over,

we now have that via delay
increasing to eight picoseconds.

Now, three picoseconds
and eight picoseconds
might not sound like very much

until you consider what
is the SKU tolerance
that you're trying to match to.

So the value of 50 picoseconds
that I put up on the board
is the SKU relative to the clock.

But the byte lane SKU can
actually be much higher,
it can be lower than 50 picoseconds.
So what that means is just one
of these eight picosecond vias
could eat up a lot of the margin

that you have available on
that bus for SKU tolerance.

So it really is a good idea to
include this via delay value

when you're trying to delay
match high speed buses,
assuming you know what the delay value is.

Now, in order to apply
that via delay value,

it's actually very easy
to do it inside of Altium.
When you are inside of Altium,

just open up the PCB
that you're working on,

go over to the via in
question and select the via.
Go over to the Properties panel,

and you'll see here there's an
entry for propagation delay.
All you have to do is just enter in

the calculated propagation
delay value into this field

and it's going to include that
value in your length tuning
or delay tuning calculations.
So to summarize, as long as the via delay

does not use up too
much of your SKU margin,
you don't need to include it
inside of your delay tuning calculation.

However, if that via delay
is a considerable fraction
of your SKU margin, you should include it
and make sure that it is accounted for
when your CAD tool does delay tuning.

In another video, we'll look
at an analysis of S parameters,

and I'll show you how to get
a propagation delay value
from an insertion loss plot.

Until then, make sure to
hit the Subscribe button,
hit the Like button,

leave your comments and questions
in the comments section,

and, of course, don't forget
to call your fabricator folks,
and we'll see you in the next video.
